cases.scene_type: cemetery epitaph survey restores a life from weathered words
cases.title_en: Tide Keeper's Stone: A Rubbing Restores the Record
cases.prompt_en: A historic cemetery on a breezy hill. At one weathered headstone, a conservator in a beige work apron kneels on a padded mat, smoothing acid-free paper over the carved face and rubbing it with a wax crayon. Beside her, an assistant holds open a heavy burial ledger. On a portable research board, a handwritten letter and a note card are clipped, and a small green conservation stake stands at the grave. Text on weathered headstone in Rowan Hill Cemetery reads exactly: "EMILIA ROSS · KEEPER OF THE TIDE CLOCK · STILLED ONLY AT THE LAST BELL · AGED 65 YEARS · THE HARBOR KNEW HER HOURS". Text on open burial ledger reads exactly: "PLOT 27 · EMILIA ROSS · DIED 19 APRIL 1906 · AGE 65 · HEART FAILURE · STONE SET 1907 · DAUGHTER M. HALE". Text on letter clipped to research board reads exactly: "Dear Archivist, my great-aunt tended the harbor clock for forty years. The stone says tide keeper; the ledger may set it right.". Text on note card clipped to research board reads exactly: "Rubbing supports only EMILIA ROSS. Ledger records 'harbor clock' on the old pier. No source calls her tide keeper; treat as dedication, not occupation.". Text on small green conservation stake at grave reads exactly: "ROWAN HILL CEMETERY CONSERVATION · EMILIA ROSS · PLOT 27". The conservator pulls the rubbing paper taut, letting worn letters darken on the page. The assistant angles the ledger toward the light, then taps a line with a gloved finger. The conservator compares the stone, the ledger, and the letter, then writes a careful line on the note card, separating the epitaph's poetic phrase from documented fact.

cases.scene_type: wrestling-mask embroidery attribution and program correction
cases.prompt_en:
In a dimly lit independent wrestling gym, three figures gather around a workbench: a retired luchador in a faded robe, a master mask maker with magnifying loupes, and a younger former assistant. On the table lies a vibrant, repaired wrestling mask with a prominent silver star motif. Beside it are embroidery sample strips showing distinct thread textures, a yellowed bout program from 1998, a leather-bound work notebook, and a fresh white display card. The group is examining the mask's construction, specifically the stitching of the star, to resolve a historical attribution error. Text on Faded bout program from 1998, lying flat on the table reads exactly: "MAIN EVENT: EL SOLAR vs. LA LUNA
Costume Credit: El Solar (Design & Stitch)
Date: Nov 14, 1998". Text on Leather-bound work notebook, open to a page with handwritten notes reads exactly: "Nov 12, 1998: Master asked me to finish the star. I used the double-knot he taught me. Its tension is tighter than his style. I signed the inside hem with my initials, but he never credited me.". Text on Embroidery sample strip pinned to the mask reads exactly: "Sample A: Master's Standard Knot
Sample B: Assistant's Double-Knot (Tighter Tension)". Text on White display card for the anniversary exhibition reads exactly: "El Solar's 1998 Championship Mask
Design: El Solar
Stitching: Mateo (Assistant)
Restored & Verified: 2024
Signed: [Master's Signature] [Mateo's Signature]". The assistant points to a specific thread join on the mask, matching it to a sample strip. The master maker opens the notebook to a page with handwritten notes. The retired performer reads the old program, then looks at the new display card. They discuss the evidence, acknowledging the assistant's skill. Finally, the assistant and the master maker sign the corrected display card together, while the retired performer nods in agreement, validating the shared credit. cases.scene_type: painted stage scenery restoration uncovers a hidden signature
cases.title_en: A Name Under the Forest Floor
cases.prompt_en:
In the lofty restoration workshop of a small repertory theatre, an enormous hand-painted woodland backdrop lies flat on the floor, its linen surface held taut by wooden battens and felt pads. Conservators in aprons kneel on rolling boards, working with cotton swabs and solvent around the painted trees and undergrowth. On a wheeled trolley at the edge are aged paper inventory records, small tins of paint samples with tie-on labels, and a fresh sheet of paper clipped to a wooden board. Text on handwritten note and signature exposed under overpaint in the lower right corner of the backdrop reads exactly: "With M. Delacroix for the crown and sky, I, W. N. Lane, painted the glades and leaf work. A. Voss cut in the birch trunks. The stage manager asked us to keep our names from the playbill.". Text on aged production inventory card on the restoration trolley reads exactly: "1937 Inventory
Riverside Repertory
Hamlet, Act 4
Forest and Glade
Scenery painted by M. Delacroix
Costumes S. Feld
Lighting R. Kim". Text on tie-on labels on small pigment sample tins reads exactly: "L-4 emerald green over lead white, crown. L-7 ochre and burnt umber, glade. L-12 iron black under resin brown, birch.". Text on new attribution sheet clipped to a board on the trolley reads exactly: "Attribution corrected 2024. M. Delacroix composed the design; W. N. Lane and A. Voss executed the glades and woodland floor.". A conservator wets a swab at the lower right area of the drop and slowly rubs the grimy overpaint. Beneath it, handwriting emerges with a signature. She pauses, uses a clean cloth to soften the area, then reads the revealed lines aloud to a colleague. Her colleague lifts the inventory card, matches the single credit against the hidden statement, and carries both to the trolley. He picks up the corrected attribution sheet, adds a date, and slides it into the production record binder.

cases.scene_type: tattoo motif consent and lineage consultation
cases.prompt_en:
In a quiet tattoo studio, a client, their aunt, and an artist gather around a drafting table. They examine a sketchbook containing a family crest, a tracing overlay with red annotations, a consent worksheet, and a final stencil label. The artist uses a pen to cross out a symbol on the overlay and redraws a border line. The aunt and client review the changes and prepare to sign the document. 

1. A large open sketchbook page with a hand-drawn crest displays clear, legible text: "Source: Great-Aunt Elara’s 1920 Diary. Elements: Oak branch (resilience), River wave (origin). Note: These shapes are inherited memory. Do not alter the core geometry."
2. A tracing overlay with red ink annotations displays clear, legible text: "REVISION: Remove 'Star' symbol. No evidence in family records. Redraw border to match original curvature. Artist adds this flourish; it is not ancestral."
3. A white consent worksheet with a clear header and signature lines displays legible text: "Lineage Consent Form. I confirm the design respects our history. I authorize reproduction on skin only. No commercial use. Initials: ______ (Aunt) ______ (Client)"
4. A small label on the final stencil sheet displays legible text: "Stencil V2. Approved 14 Oct. For single use only. Do not distribute."

The artist points to a specific symbol on the tracing overlay, explaining it lacks historical basis. The aunt nods, confirming the removal. The artist then redraws the outer border to match the original sketch. Finally, both the aunt and the client pick up pens to initial the revised consent worksheet, authorizing the new design.

cases.scene_type: documentary edit reconciles transcript, consent and narration
cases.prompt_en: A documentary editing room at dusk. Two editors sit at a wide light table with a long column of paper transcript strips from an oral history. Beside the strips lie a narration draft page with a sentence circled in black ink, a small pink consent card from the narrator, and a spiral-bound ethical edit log. A clay bowl paperweight holds the strips open; red and blue pencils rest on a tray. Text on Transcript strip reads exactly: "MARTA: The neighbors said the bakery was haunted. They meant my grandmother sang after midnight in the flour room. It was the only hour the ovens were hers, and she sang the lullabies her mother brought from Tres Ríos. The singing was not a ghost. It was her remembering in the only place they let her work. When I tell this story, I want the oven hour, not the ghost.". Text on Narration draft page reads exactly: "NARRATION 7 DRAFT: The old bakery was haunted by a voice that came from nowhere, a ghost who sang before dawn. The sound was beautiful, and no one could explain it.". Text on Consent note card reads exactly: "I, Marta Reino, give permission for my words to be used only in full context and never arranged so they sound like someone else's story.". Text on Ethical edit log reads exactly: "EDIT LOG — Narration 7: removed 'a ghost who sang before dawn.' Marta's transcript, lines 12–14, shows the singing was her grandmother's memory of the ovens, not a specter. Restored the sentence 'It was her remembering in the only place they let her work.' Ask Marta to approve before the final cut.". One editor lifts the circled line from the narration draft and lays it over the transcript strip where the memory first appears. After reading the two texts together, the other editor draws a red line through the circled sentence, writes a dated note in the ethical edit log, and turns the consent card so its underlined condition faces the corrected strip.

required_text.verbatim: MARTA: The neighbors said the bakery was haunted. They meant my grandmother sang after midnight in the flour room. It was the only hour the ovens were hers, and she sang the lullabies her mother brought from Tres Ríos. The singing was not a ghost. It was her remembering in the only place they let her work. When I tell this story, I want the oven hour, not the ghost.

required_text.role: The narrator's full memory, which restores the meaning of the phrase the draft had removed.

required_text.verbatim: NARRATION 7 DRAFT: The old bakery was haunted by a voice that came from nowhere, a ghost who sang before dawn. The sound was beautiful, and no one could explain it.

required_text.role: The misleading line, cut from the narrator's memory, that the editors remove once the full context is restored.

required_text.verbatim: I, Marta Reino, give permission for my words to be used only in full context and never arranged so they sound like someone else's story.
required_text.form: handwritten note on a pink index card with the final condition underlined
required_text.role: The narrator's consent condition, which the edit log cites as the standard for restoring the sentence.

required_text.verbatim: EDIT LOG — Narration 7: removed 'a ghost who sang before dawn.' Marta's transcript, lines 12–14, shows the singing was her grandmother's memory of the ovens, not a specter. Restored the sentence 'It was her remembering in the only place they let her work.' Ask Marta to approve before the final cut.

The printer lifts a pencil note from under the proof sheet, sets it beside the diary, checks the ledger entry, then turns the proof press. A clean sheet is lifted and read against the pinned proof.

cases.scene_type: maritime logbook and signal flags resolve a rescue story
cases.title_en: The Signal That Turned the Mabel H.
cases.prompt_en: In the low-ceiled workroom of a coastal heritage trust, two archivists and a retired pilot stand around a long oak table. One side holds an open signal-chest with rolled flags and cork floats; the table holds an open keeper's logbook surrounded by a code card, a typed letter, and a small chalkboard. A short halyard is strung across the room for indoor flag hoisting. The room smells faintly of tar, ink, and old paper. Text on open keeper's logbook reads exactly: "18 March 1937. South wind freshening, sea rough, glass falling. At 14:40 the coaster Mabel H. raised two flags close together: red over yellow, and a black square. I read red-over-yellow as a tow fault and answered with the storm cone. She wore north before dark came down. At 17:44 her mast light vanished under Gull Rock. I held to the old code and lost her. Keeper A. Calder.". Text on laminated code card reads exactly: "1912 Coast Code, Wreck Card No. 4 — hoist as one string, read lower flag first: red over yellow = boat disabled, require tow; black square = anchor dragging; storm cone = harbor closed, no entry.". Text on typed survivor's letter reads exactly: "Dear Mr. Calder, I am Elias Voss, mate of the Mabel H. My captain took your cone as a closed harbor and wore north. I knew the old card said red over yellow was disabled, not a tow fault. The card hung by the binnacle, but nobody touched it after 1930. I am sending you that page. We lost two men off Gull Rock. I do not blame you; I blame the years we trusted memory over the printed code. I hope the next keeper reads the card first. Respectfully, Elias Voss.". Text on small chalkboard reads exactly: "14:40 – Mabel H. hoists red/yellow + black square. 14:52 – storm cone raised. 15:10 – Mabel H. turns north. 17:44 – mast light lost. Corrected reading: red/yellow means disabled, cone should not have gone up.". One archivist points to a line in the open log, then turns the code card so its flag sequence faces up, and taps the typed letter. The retired pilot lifts two small folded signal flags from the chest, clips them to the indoor halyard, and raises them side by side. Another person erases one chalk line on the board and writes a fresh line above the old times. The visible writing reveals how the navigational mistake was read and corrected.

required_text.verbatim: 18 March 1937. South wind freshening, sea rough, glass falling. At 14:40 the coaster Mabel H. raised two flags close together: red over yellow, and a black square. I read red-over-yellow as a tow fault and answered with the storm cone. She wore north before dark came down. At 17:44 her mast light vanished under Gull Rock. I held to the old code and lost her. Keeper A. Calder.
required_text.role: original record containing the mistaken code reading

required_text.verbatim: 1912 Coast Code, Wreck Card No. 4 — hoist as one string, read lower flag first: red over yellow = boat disabled, require tow; black square = anchor dragging; storm cone = harbor closed, no entry.
required_text.role: code key that exposes the logbook misinterpretation

required_text.verbatim: Dear Mr. Calder, I am Elias Voss, mate of the Mabel H. My captain took your cone as a closed harbor and wore north. I knew the old card said red over yellow was disabled, not a tow fault. The card hung by the binnacle, but nobody touched it after 1930. I am sending you that page. We lost two men off Gull Rock. I do not blame you; I blame the years we trusted memory over the printed code. I hope the next keeper reads the card first. Respectfully, Elias Voss.
required_text.role: later testimony that corrects and completes the log entry

cases.scene_type: costume atelier reconstructs an uncredited performer's coat
cases.prompt_en: A small costume atelier in the late afternoon. On a dress form stands a worn burgundy velvet evening coat with one shoulder sitting slightly higher than the other. The worktable holds spread pattern paper with red pencil marks, an open ledger, a handwritten letter, and a small museum label. Measuring tape, shears, and spools of thread rest near the fabric shelves. Text on handwritten letter pinned beside the dress form reads exactly: "Dear Mrs. Hale, please keep the extra two inches at the shoulder and the deep side pocket for my script. I know the programme leaves me out, but the coat remembers. I wore it ninety-one times under the blue light. Yours, Elinor Voss.". Text on open wardrobe ledger page reads exactly: "Wardrobe Ledger 1937–38. Burgundy velvet coat — worn by Miss E. Voss, understudy, 91 performances. Altered: shoulder +2in, deep side pocket. No programme credit.". Text on red-pencil note on pattern paper reads exactly: "Add 2in to shoulder — E.V.". Text on corrected exhibition label reads exactly: "Evening coat. Worn by Elinor Voss, understudy at the Corinth Theatre, 1937–1938. She performed ninety-one nights; the coat is the archive the programme erased.". A costume maker lifts the folded letter from the coat's deep side pocket, reads it through, then checks the open ledger and measures the coat's shoulder against the pattern. She traces the red pencil note with her finger, nods, and fastens a corrected exhibition label to the lining.

cases.title_en: The Quay That Changed the Step
cases.prompt_en: A community hall with a worn wooden floor and folding chairs along one wall. A low stand stands beside a long chalk drawing on the floor; an open notebook rests on the stand, and a separate narrow rhythm card is taped strictly to the front edge of the stand. On the floor, chalk route labels and arrows mark two paths side by side; at the start of the route a small correction card is propped upright, showing only a version code and source line. An older teacher and three adult dancers in socks gather around the floor marks; the low stand is placed so the rhythm card and both chalk paths are visible together. Text on chalk route labels drawn on the wooden floor reads exactly: "OLD PATH — heel-cut step / NEW PATH — ball-lift step". Text on narrow rhythm-syllable card taped to the front edge of the low stand reads exactly: "bom · pa · TA-TA / soft · up · hold". Text on handwritten page in an open notebook resting on the low stand reads exactly: "When my mother left Fuen in the dry year, the ship's deck was too crowded for the heel-beat, so on the quay at Bruma she changed it to a soft ball step. She always said the sea gave the dance a new footfall. I teach the phrase as she passed it: quiet on the downbeat, lift on the turn.". Text on correction card propped upright at the start of the chalk route reads exactly: "LINE 6 / OLD HEEL-CUT = SHORE VERSION / B8 BALL-LIFT = HARBOR VERSION / SOURCE: ÁUREA MATOS, BRUMA, 1962". The teacher crouches and points at the correction card, then firmly stamps her heel into the wood to demonstrate the old footfall; immediately after, she repeats the phrase with a soft, distinct lift of her forefoot to demonstrate the new step. The three dancers watch her feet closely, glance at the narrow rhythm card on the stand, and follow the two chalk paths across the floor. One dancer touches the edge of the correction card while passing.

required_text.verbatim: When my mother left Fuen in the dry year, the ship's deck was too crowded for the heel-beat, so on the quay at Bruma she changed it to a soft ball step. She always said the sea gave the dance a new footfall. I teach the phrase as she passed it: quiet on the downbeat, lift on the turn.
required_text.role: explains the migration memory behind the changed step

required_text.role: corrects and attributes the older step as a shore version

cases.scene_type: independent comic page rewritten through lettering
cases.title_en: The Tin Bridge: Second Lettering Pass
cases.prompt_en: In a softly lit comics studio, an oversized page of the comic being revised is pinned to a corkboard. Mara Venn, the writer-artist, kneels by the board with a blue pencil; Jules Okonkwo, the letterer, sits at a low table with pens, brushes, a jar of ink, and sheets of translucent overlay paper. The page is covered with penciled panels, word balloons, margin notes, and small pieces of drafting tape. On the table are several alternative lettering studies on slips of paper. Text on drafting tape header at the top of the pinned page reads exactly: "THE TIN BRIDGE — PAGE 14 — SECOND LETTERING PASS — INK STUDY — MARA VENN & JULES OKONKWO — 7 MAY". Text on blue-pencil deletion in the original balloon of panel 4 reads exactly: "the box only whispered salt". Text on Jules's revised dialogue balloon on translucent overlay, taped over the lower panel reads exactly: "Mother kept the storm in a tin box. Every raindrop was a ticket stub. I found the key under the bridge, but the box smelled of harbor smoke. I am learning to read that smell.". Text on Mara's blue-pencil margin note beside the overlay reads exactly: "Move monologue to panel 6. Let panel 4 stay empty. Keep 'tin box' tight, let 'harbor smoke' be loose and low.". Text on small ink-stained slip pinned beneath panel 4 reads exactly: "Old SFX: KLANG. New SFX: ktooong — low tail. Place under panel 4, after the pause.". Mara crosses out an earlier line in the original word balloon with blue pencil and tapes Jules's revised overlay over the lower panel. Jules lifts the overlay, reads the monologue once, then adds a margin note about moving the text to a later panel. Mara nods, erases the old sound effect in the fourth panel, and watches Jules write the new onomatopoeia below it. Jules also attaches a separate slip with lettering instructions next to the monologue. Together they adjust the pacing by choosing which words stay tight and which are allowed to loosen.

required_text.carrier: drafting tape header at the top of the pinned page
required_text.verbatim: THE TIN BRIDGE — PAGE 14 — SECOND LETTERING PASS — INK STUDY — MARA VENN & JULES OKONKWO — 7 MAY
required_text.role: identifies the page, pass, contributors, and date of the lettering study

required_text.carrier: blue-pencil deletion in the original balloon of panel 4
required_text.verbatim: the box only whispered salt
required_text.role: records the phrase replaced by the revised monologue; the deletion is the evidence of the correction

required_text.verbatim: Mother kept the storm in a tin box. Every raindrop was a ticket stub. I found the key under the bridge, but the box smelled of harbor smoke. I am learning to read that smell.
required_text.role: the character's relettered monologue; its new closing image replaces the crossed-out line and carries the emotional turn of the page

required_text.carrier: Mara's blue-pencil margin note beside the overlay
required_text.verbatim: Move monologue to panel 6. Let panel 4 stay empty. Keep 'tin box' tight, let 'harbor smoke' be loose and low.
required_text.role: gives the correction context: the monologue is moved, and the lettering shapes the two key images differently

required_text.role: changes the page's audible moment by replacing a final clang with a ringing sound that continues after a pause

cases.scene_type: stop-motion archive restores intent from exposure sheets
cases.prompt_en:
In a softly lit animation archive, an archivist's bench holds a small stop-motion puppet of a young woman in a traveling coat, a miniature valise, a compartmentalized tray of numbered mouth shapes, a typed exposure sheet under a brass paperweight, and a faded letter flattened beside a small door model. Text on exposure sheet reads exactly: "SEC 07 — MARA AT THE DOOR — TAKE 11
FRAME 96 — MOUTH 3 — LIP-SYNC: 'I will come back before the ice breaks.'
ACTION: 'Left hand lifts the valise; right hand turns the latch.'
TAKE 9 NOTE: 'The hand dropped at 96; with the hand dropped, the scene closes in on itself.'
RESTORED: 'Take 11 keeps the latch turn; the leaving becomes a choice, not an ending.'
FRAME 118 — MOUTH 7 — LIP-SYNC: 'The road will hold.'". Text on animator's letter reads exactly: "Dear Sol,

I keep looking at take 9. Mara's hand drops at 96 and the whole scene turns inward. Take 11 is the one I meant: she turns the latch, lifts the valise, and walks toward the road. Please do not flatten the gesture. The goodbye is a beginning.

Signed,
Wren". Text on restoration decision note reads exactly: "RESTORATION NOTE: Compare 1967 take 11 with take 9. The frame 96 latch turn matches Wren's letter, so keep it. Mark take 9 as alternate; do not let it cancel the goodbye. Catalogue entry: restored by Tali, July 2023, hinge not replaced.". Text on mouth tray label reads exactly: "THE LONG EXPECTED HARBOUR
MARA REPLACEMENT MOUTHS
SET 12
96: 3 / 118: 7 / 122: 2". An archivist in cotton gloves reads the typed sheet, then the letter, chooses one of the numbered mouth shapes, fits it to the puppet's face, and sets the puppet's right hand against the miniature door's latch before easing the figure forward a step.

required_text.verbatim:
SEC 07 — MARA AT THE DOOR — TAKE 11
FRAME 96 — MOUTH 3 — LIP-SYNC: 'I will come back before the ice breaks.'
ACTION: 'Left hand lifts the valise; right hand turns the latch.'
TAKE 9 NOTE: 'The hand dropped at 96; with the hand dropped, the scene closes in on itself.'
RESTORED: 'Take 11 keeps the latch turn; the leaving becomes a choice, not an ending.'
FRAME 118 — MOUTH 7 — LIP-SYNC: 'The road will hold.'
required_text.form: typed exposure sheet with pencilled corrections
required_text.role: frame-action record and restored intent

required_text.verbatim:
Dear Sol,

I keep looking at take 9. Mara's hand drops at 96 and the whole scene turns inward. Take 11 is the one I meant: she turns the latch, lifts the valise, and walks toward the road. Please do not flatten the gesture. The goodbye is a beginning.

Signed,
Wren
required_text.role: animator's original intention

required_text.verbatim: RESTORATION NOTE: Compare 1967 take 11 with take 9. The frame 96 latch turn matches Wren's letter, so keep it. Mark take 9 as alternate; do not let it cancel the goodbye. Catalogue entry: restored by Tali, July 2023, hinge not replaced.
required_text.role: decision record

required_text.verbatim:
THE LONG EXPECTED HARBOUR
MARA REPLACEMENT MOUTHS
SET 12
96: 3 / 118: 7 / 122: 2

cases.scene_type: community soundwalk turns field notes into a shared map
cases.title_en: The Street That Held Two Names
cases.prompt_en: In a bright community hall, five neighbors gather around a large printed street map spread across a worktable. The map is marked with numbered listening stations, a small printed route card clipped to its lower edge, and a handwritten field-note page set near the fourth station. A woman in a knitted vest gestures toward the alley; a man holds a coil of headphones, and a younger resident keeps a sticky note balanced on the map's edge. Text on handwritten field-note page set near the fourth station reads exactly: "At station 4 the fishmonger's bell calls the same hour my mother heard it in 1962. I stood at the corner and wrote the name from her mouth: Katel Alley, not Kettle. The kettle hiss was the tea shop vent.". Text on small printed route card clipped to the map's lower edge reads exactly: "Route: start at ST1 beside the bakery, pause at ST3 under the clock, finish where the alley stops sounding.". Text on printed station-label list along the map margin reads exactly: "ST1 bakery door • ST3 clock tower • ST4 fish bell, kettle hiss, iron grate • ST5 cart rattle". Text on handwritten sticky note balanced on the map's edge reads exactly: "The map printed one name, my neighbor heard another. I will trust her voice.". One resident pins the handwritten field note to the map. Another traces a penciled route line from the first station to the third and then pauses at the fourth, where the younger resident places the sticky note next to the printed place name. The group leans in as the older resident speaks.

required_text.verbatim: At station 4 the fishmonger's bell calls the same hour my mother heard it in 1962. I stood at the corner and wrote the name from her mouth: Katel Alley, not Kettle. The kettle hiss was the tea shop vent.
required_text.role: old-resident testimony that corrects the printed map name

required_text.role: guides walkers through the labeled listening stations

cases.scene_type: board-game club reconstructs rules from an incomplete set
cases.title_en: The Missing Rule at the Long Table
cases.prompt_en: Inside a wood-paneled community hall, a board-game club sits around a long table spread with a wool blanket. An open game box stands at one end; beside it lies the sea-map board with painted islands, wooden sailor tokens, small brass bells, and grey fog counters. Around the board are several paper documents: a torn printed booklet leaf, a handwritten house-rule scrap, a tournament record sheet, and a proposal card with pencil marks. Text on printed rule leaflet from the original game booklet reads exactly: "Rule 7 — The three lamps of Coracle Bell. They must be lit before dawn on the same island. If fog tokens outnumber the lamps, the sailor token is carried to the far reef. The crew loses one shared resource, and the story continues from the next year. The ferry token returns to the harbor at the turn after the rescue.". Text on handwritten scrap of paper reads exactly: "House rule, Red Lamp Club, 1979: if a page is missing, every player writes the number they remember. We keep the smallest number until the tournament sheet returns.". Text on carbon-copy tournament record sheet reads exactly: "North Harbor Tournament, 1988 — Round 4. Fog came before the third move. Judge Marta ruled from the missing page: count fog only after the third move, and one bell may be spent to see the tide map. Rescue cost was doubled.". Text on proposed reconstruction card reads exactly: "Proposed reconstruction — Rule 7a. Count fog only after the third move. A crew may spend one bell token to view the tide map before deciding. This follows the 1988 judge's record.". Text on pencil note on the reconstruction card reads exactly: "Accepted 4 Nov. — page 4 restored.". A player places the proposal card beside the printed booklet leaf and taps the tournament record sheet. Another player unfolds the handwritten house-rule scrap between them, comparing it with the proposal. The group sets three bell tokens on one painted island, then adds grey fog counters; when the grey counters overtake the bells, a player moves the wooden sailor token to a reef space. A fourth player writes an acceptance note on the proposal card, then tucks it back into the torn spine of the booklet.

required_text.verbatim: Rule 7 — The three lamps of Coracle Bell. They must be lit before dawn on the same island. If fog tokens outnumber the lamps, the sailor token is carried to the far reef. The crew loses one shared resource, and the story continues from the next year. The ferry token returns to the harbor at the turn after the rescue.

required_text.role: surviving original rule that anchors the reconstruction

required_text.role: local variation from memory

required_text.form: typed tournament record with handwritten round number
required_text.role: official record that preserves the lost wording

required_text.verbatim: Proposed reconstruction — Rule 7a. Count fog only after the third move. A crew may spend one bell token to view the tide map before deciding. This follows the 1988 judge's record.
required_text.form: typed proposal card with penciled annotations
required_text.role: reasoned restoration tested against the physical pieces

required_text.carrier: pencil note on the reconstruction card
required_text.verbatim: Accepted 4 Nov. — page 4 restored.

required_text.role: club verdict that closes the reconstruction

cases.prompt_en:
In a quiet community archive room, three older men gather around a bright light table. Spread out are four 1980s photo-booth strips, a yellowed coat-check ticket, a handwritten diary page, and a typed archival label. The group is debating the provenance of the images. One man points to a specific frame, another holds up the ticket, and a third writes on a correction slip. The atmosphere is collaborative but cautious. 

1. A white typed archival label attached to the photo strip sleeve reads exactly: "ITEM 84-B: Farewell Party, The Velvet Room, June 1986. Subjects: Unknown regulars. Note: Date confirmed by manager."
2. A yellowed paper coat-check ticket reads exactly: "THE VELVET ROOM. COAT CHECK #402. DATE: 12 NOV 86. TIME: 11:45 PM. RETURN TO DESK."
3. A handwritten note on the back of the photo strip reads exactly: "Not the goodbye. This was the night we found the broken jukebox. Sarah wore the red jacket. Please blur face #3."
4. A typed correction slip for the public catalog reads exactly: "REVISED CAPTION: The Velvet Room, Nov 1986. Regulars after hours. Note: Identity of third subject withheld per contributor request."
5. A small sticky note on the diary page reads exactly: "Check ticket #402."

The participants compare the visual evidence of the photo strips against the written records. They identify a mismatch between the archived date and the coat-check ticket. One contributor requests that a face in the third frame be obscured for privacy. The group agrees on a corrected caption that acknowledges the uncertainty and the specific event, then signs the consent form to update the public record.

required_text.role: Physical evidence contradicting the archival label's date.

cases.scene_type: migrant diner memory reconstructed from menu and receipts
cases.prompt_en: Inside a community hall, a temporary installation rebuilds the counter of a fictional all-night diner. A worn wooden counter, chrome stools, a chalkboard menu on a stand, a corkboard holding a letter and receipts, and a glass case containing one small pale-purple yam tuber with smooth, firm skin and no branching rootlets. Two former customers sit at the counter with their coats on; a retired cook in a stained apron stands behind it. Penciled index cards are taped near a napkin dispenser, and a shoe box holds more cards. A small basket on the counter holds several more dry pale-purple yam tubers, the same compact, smooth-skinned shape as the specimen under glass. A single warm lamp casts a pool of light across the counter. Text on a handwritten letter pinned to a corkboard, written on lined notebook paper reads exactly: "I am from a tin town. At Mariam's stall I found a pale purple root and remembered my aunt's yam soup. I bought a sack. My first customers wrinkled their noses. I roasted it with garlic and palm oil, and by spring everyone ordered Quiet Root Stew, though the true name was still unknown.". Text on a small brown-paper receipt pinned beside the letter, with torn perforated edge reads exactly: "MARIAM'S TROPICAL PROVISIONS — 18 JAN 1988 / 2 sacks purple yams, 14 lb / 1 bottle palm oil / 5 lb chickpeas / bitter greens / total $11.20 — PAID". Text on a chalkboard menu standing on the counter, with a handwritten correction over the first line reads exactly: "HAN'S LATE NIGHT / WINTER 1988 / Quiet Root Stew over rice — $3.50 / Fish sauce eggs — $2.00 / Bitter greens with garlic — $1.75 / Tea, always free". Text on an index card taped above the napkin dispenser, handwriting in pencil reads exactly: "Every Tuesday after the 4 a.m. streetcar I ate the stew. It tasted like my grandmother's mountain. Years later Mariam's stall had a paper sign: 'Lila yam from the highlands.' That is how the root got its true name.". The retired cook pins the supplier receipt beside a handwritten letter on the corkboard, then turns the chalkboard menu so the patrons can read it. One patron points at the menu, picks up an index card taped above the napkin dispenser, and reads it. The other patron pulls a paper sign from the shoe box that gives the root's later name, places a small basket of pale-purple yam tubers on the counter, and aligns one compact pale-purple tuber with the paper sign and the brown-paper receipt. The cook nods and adds a penciled note to the menu's first line.

required_text.carrier: a handwritten letter pinned to a corkboard, written on lined notebook paper
required_text.verbatim: I am from a tin town. At Mariam's stall I found a pale purple root and remembered my aunt's yam soup. I bought a sack. My first customers wrinkled their noses. I roasted it with garlic and palm oil, and by spring everyone ordered Quiet Root Stew, though the true name was still unknown.
required_text.role: Cook's testimony about inventing the dish before its true name was known.

required_text.carrier: a small brown-paper receipt pinned beside the letter, with torn perforated edge
required_text.verbatim: MARIAM'S TROPICAL PROVISIONS — 18 JAN 1988 / 2 sacks purple yams, 14 lb / 1 bottle palm oil / 5 lb chickpeas / bitter greens / total $11.20 — PAID
required_text.role: Evidence that the purple yams were sold under a trade name at the same stall, prompting the later correction.

required_text.carrier: a chalkboard menu standing on the counter, with a handwritten correction over the first line
required_text.verbatim: HAN'S LATE NIGHT / WINTER 1988 / Quiet Root Stew over rice — $3.50 / Fish sauce eggs — $2.00 / Bitter greens with garlic — $1.75 / Tea, always free
required_text.role: Shows the dish's public nickname and price, anchoring the memory.

cases.prompt_en:
In a small rehearsal studio, a Deaf storyteller, a movement editor and a young co-author stand around a waist-high table covered with numbered story cards. A wall projection mirrors the performer's signing as colored floor marks identify where each character's viewpoint begins. Text on a large rehearsal note pinned beside the mirrored signing projection reads exactly: "THE RED KITE — REVISION 6
The child narrates the crossing, not the elder. Keep the kite in the child's signing space until the bridge line ends. The change restores Mira's viewpoint and clarifies the final handoff.". On the table, a large, legible numbered gloss card 14 reads exactly: "CARD 14
CHILD IX-a | KITE IX-b
BRIDGE CROSS CONTINUE
ELDER WATCH IX-a
HAND-OFF KITE: child space → elder space". Beside it, a young co-author's handwritten correction strip is large and legible, reading exactly: "My line begins before the bridge. Please keep CHILD as narrator through Card 14. The elder receives the kite only after the pause. — Mira". A revised authorship and consent card clipped to the script folder is visible, reading exactly: "Story: Mira Vale + Jon Osei
Signed performance: Jon Osei
Spatial edit approved: Mira MV / Jon JO / Editor SK
Use this revision for the community rehearsal only.". The storyteller stops at the disputed card, moves the narrator marker from the elder character to the child character, repeats the passage with the corrected spatial reference, and asks both collaborators to initial the revised authorship card.

cases.scene_type: book repair traces a volume through ownership inscriptions
cases.title_en: The Coast Road in the Endpapers
cases.prompt_en: An open travel volume rests on a padded cradle on a conservator's workbench. The front flyleaf carries a dark ink passage with a paler pencil reply beneath it; near the spine fold lies a loose page section. A needle and thread lie on the bench beside a stack of blank repair labels. Text on Front flyleaf of the travel volume reads exactly: "Perla Navarre bought this book in Torremuelle on 14 May 1932, the day the mule road washed out. I carried it over the cliff stair to Serpent Bay and read it aloud to my father, who had walked the same coast forty years earlier. He laughed at the compass sketch, saying the iron fence was never there. I keep it because the route is already changing and the book will know what I remembered.". Text on Margin below the first-owner passage, same flyleaf reads exactly: "R. March, 1961: The cliff stair is a rubble line now. I walked it with the book in hand, and found the iron fence just as she remembered, hidden under blackberry. The old name was Ciego Gate.". Text on Pasted slip in the rear pastedown reads exactly: "Merrow Public Library. Accession 4417. Gift of Ruth March, 1963. Shelved Travel, Case 9. Inscribed 'not to be lent.'". Text on Tipped-in repair label near the spine fold reads exactly: "Conservation repair by Tamsin Voss, July 1984. Re-sewn through three signatures. Removed adhesive tape from the facing page. All ink inscriptions preserved.". The conservator tilts the flyleaf toward the lamp to follow the ink passage, then the pencil reply. She checks the printed accession slip in the rear pastedown, returns the loose pages to their original order, and sews through the first signature. She then writes a dated repair label and sets it beside the book.

required_text.verbatim: Perla Navarre bought this book in Torremuelle on 14 May 1932, the day the mule road washed out. I carried it over the cliff stair to Serpent Bay and read it aloud to my father, who had walked the same coast forty years earlier. He laughed at the compass sketch, saying the iron fence was never there. I keep it because the route is already changing and the book will know what I remembered.

cases.scene_type: incarcerated writers prepare a consent-led anthology proof
cases.prompt_en: Inside a modest print room at a fictional correctional education center, adult writers and their editor work around a long table covered with loose proof pages and a cover sheet. A printed policy placard is mounted on the wall. The atmosphere is quiet and attentive. Text on handwritten note clipped to the margin of a proof page reads exactly: "I wrote this letter to my sister the year I could not send it. I have changed the names of the children and the place. Please keep my mother's garden out of the book. I want readers to know I am a baker now, not a number.". Text on printed policy placard on the wall reads exactly: "Every piece appears only with the author's signed consent. No name is printed unless the author chooses it. Words may be revised only by the person who wrote them.". Text on cover sheet of the anthology proof reads exactly: "Voices from Room 4 / Second Proof / Marlow Correctional Education Workshop / Seventeen Writers". Text on attribution line on the contents page reads exactly: "Denise Whitfield — name shown? No — pen name: D.W. — title: The Unsent Letter". One writer taps the handwritten margin note, then signs the permission line beneath it. The editor compares the chosen name line with the wall placard. Another writer presses a rubber stamp onto the proof cover while the group watches.

cases.scene_type: illustrated story scroll unfolds during oral narration
cases.title_en: The Scroll That Lets the Smallest Ask
cases.prompt_en: In a lamplit reading room of a small harbor library, an elderly storyteller and a younger illustrator unroll a long painted paper scroll across a low oak table. A small audience sits on cushions and stools around the table. The scroll has hand-painted panels with short ink labels, and a red ribbon bearing a repeated line hangs from one edge. A folded paper note rests inside the scroll's wooden case. Text on folded note kept inside the scroll case reads exactly: "Keep the ending light. In 1962 old Marta added a white fish and the children would not sleep until it returned. The river must give it back. Told this rule to Nor, then to me. Pass it on, but let the smallest listener ask first.". Text on ink label above a painted scroll panel reads exactly: "The goose rings the wet bell.". Text on ink label above the willow panel reads exactly: "The white fish waits under the willow.". Text on red ribbon stitched near the scroll's lower edge reads exactly: "The river answered, again, again.". Text on folded crayon note handed up by a child reads exactly: "If the goose rang the bell, did the white fish hear it above the river?". The storyteller lifts the folded note from the scroll case as the illustrator holds the far edge of the paper. She reads it aloud, then slides a finger along the painted panels, pausing at the scene where a waterbird faces a hanging bell and again where a pale fish passes beneath a willow. She resumes the tale in rhythm, flicking the refrain ribbon so it sways. A child in the audience writes on a scrap of paper, folds it, and hands it up. The storyteller reads the question, smiles, and tucks the note under the ribbon at the very end of the scroll, where the last panel is still blank.

cases.prompt_en: Two old friends sit at a kitchen table with a cassette deck, a typewritten liner note, an open spiral notebook full of song titles, a faded postcard, and a newer index card. A half-empty mug and a pen lie between them; the deck door is open and a cassette sits on the table. Text on typewritten J-card liner note reads exactly: "Lake House, 1994. The lake kept every wrong turn. You hid the oars because you were not ready to leave. I called it a lie, so you mailed me the date I refused. Play side B loud. The hiss is the water we almost lost.". Text on handwritten tracklist in spiral notebook reads exactly: "Side A: Salt on the Porch — we cracked the porch light; The Bee Line; Lantern Logic. Side B: Almost-Float; The Postcard That Lied — because the date was wrong.". Text on faded postcard reads exactly: "August 1 — I hid the oars. Not gone. Love, Lena". Text on new index-card note reads exactly: "Found the oars under the porch. The card was sent July 30 but dated Aug. 1.". Mira turns the postcard over and taps the postmark, then slides the index card to Lena. Lena reads it, compares the tracklist's last song title with the postcard, and pencils the true postmark date onto the back of the postcard. The cassette begins to play, and the two friends lean toward the speaker without speaking.

cases.scene_type: procession banner repair records a community's changing names
cases.title_en: The Banner Under Every Added Name
cases.prompt_en: Inside an enclosed upstairs community textile conservation room, four solid walls, a closed door, and a tall window separate the work space from the narrow street outside; through the window the street can be seen far below and never enters the room. A long worktable stands indoors below the window under a warm work lamp, holding three distinct text carriers: a scarlet processional banner spread flat for repair, an open steward's repair ledger set beside it, and a small route card tucked between the ledger's pages. A fourth carrier, an unstitched cloth patch, is held in a volunteer's hand above the banner's lower hem. The banner's stacked gold-thread embroidery records different group names from different decades, with each newer line sewn below the older ones, showing a collective history of names being added rather than erased. Text on Scarlet processional banner spread flat on the indoor worktable, with stacked gold-thread embroidery on scarlet cotton reads exactly: "Lantern Bearers of Eastbrook 1927 · Eastbrook Neighbors' Procession 1948 · United Lantern Fellowship 1961 · Eastbrook Lantern Walkers 1975". Text on Steward's repair ledger, open page lying on the indoor table beside the banner reads exactly: "When the weaving families left in 1961, the mill hands did not ask to replace the banner by force. They asked to be added under a truthful name. I crossed out nothing; I wrote 'Eastbrook Lantern Walkers' below the old line, and every route since has ended at Every Door.". Text on Route card tucked between the pages of the open repair ledger reads exactly: "1927 Night Lane–Quarry Gate · 1948 Night Lane–Mill Bridge · 1961 Night Lane–Weaver's Cross · 1975 Night Lane–Every Door". Text on Unstitched patch held in a volunteer's hand above the banner's lower hem reads exactly: "All who walk may carry the light". Volunteers sit around the indoor long table, keeping the scarlet banner spread flat while they repair it. One volunteer sets the open account book beside the banner so the steward's handwritten record lies under the oldest stitched line. Another volunteer draws a threaded needle through the lower hem and fixes the welcome patch below the newest embroidered name. A third volunteer slides the route card out of the ledger, lays it along the same edge of the banner, and traces the route entries from the unchanging starting lane to the final stop, making visible that the route grew after the community name was widened. All repair work, people, and text carriers remain inside the enclosed room, with the narrow street present only beyond the window glass.

cases.scene_type: postal correspondence reconstructs an indirect journey
cases.prompt_en: A wooden sorting table in a postal-history study holds five separate paper carriers: a Manila folder tab, a normal-sized sheet of personal stationery written in blue ink and lying portrait-side up, a shorter typewritten route card placed landscape at right angles to it, a returned envelope with a rubber stamp along its lower edge, and a small pencil note. The blue-ink letter is ordinary private stationery with no ruled lines, printed letterhead, columns, or postal form fields. The route card is a distinct, separate piece of paper, short in length and oriented horizontally (landscape), featuring four typewritten lines of place-and-date entries. It has absolutely no grid, no table border, no columns, and no shared backing with the letter. Two adult descendants and a postal historian lean over the objects. The historian holds the route card beside the returned envelope, comparing its typewritten places and dates with the postmarks on the envelope. A descendant slides the blue-ink letter next to the envelope so the letter's unstated clues and the route card's sequence can be cross-checked. Another descendant lifts the pencil note for the others to read. Text on Manila folder tab reads exactly: "Rovasio Correspondence — 1944-7". Text on Ordinary letter sheet written in blue ink, portrait orientation, no letterhead reads exactly: "Dear Marta, the old address is finished. I sleep near the canteen and work the night shift by the harbor wall. The men sing about three bridges but will not name this port. I draw that wall. Do not send money to Via dei Liguri; the clerk will return it.". Text on Separate short typewritten route card, landscape orientation, no grid reads exactly: "Canteen — Genova, 17 Mar; railway dormitory — Napoli, 21 Mar; harbor wall — Cagliari, 02 Apr; Returned to sender, 11 Apr". Text on Rubber stamp on returned envelope reads exactly: "RETURN TO SENDER — NO KNOWN ADDRESS AT THIS PORT". Text on Pencil note reads exactly: "He never named the town. The postmarks carried the map. For Marta, the canteen and harbor wall were the letter.". The postal historian aligns the short typewritten route card with the postmarks along the edge of the returned envelope. One descendant lifts the blue-ink letter from its portrait position and sets it beside the envelope, aligning the letter's mention of the canteen and harbor wall with the first and third lines of the route card. Another descendant picks up the pencil note and holds it above the envelope so everyone can read its conclusion. A finger traces the three port names on the route card, then stops at the rubber stamp. The descendants then place the letter, route card, and envelope into a new order on the table, making the route card reorder the letter's indirect clues into a timeline.

cases.scene_type: lost neighborhood rebuilt from residents' captioned models
cases.title_en: The Lane Takes Shape at the Table
cases.prompt_en: In a community room beside a closed library, a long table holds a low plywood model of a demolished street block. Photocopied clearance photos and a captioned planning strip lie near the edge. A handwritten index card is propped against a small cardboard bakery with a green door. A blue-pencil route loops across the painted road. Residents of different ages stand around the table, some holding toothpick labels, one adjusting a miniature fig tree in a cardboard yard. Text on handwritten index card propped against the miniature bakery reads exactly: "At No. 14 Bellwether Lane, my mother ran a bakery behind a green tin door. The alley smelled of rosemary, not oil. We sold seeded rye and kept the ovens going until the last train sounded. The Harrowgate file calls the building vacant, but I keep the ledger pages: rye, milk bread, burnt honey cake. My father weighed flour on brass scales, and the back yard had a fig tree. The window seat over the counter looked all the way down the lane, and every evening the bakery cat waited by the door.". Text on typed caption strip taped beneath a photocopied clearance photograph reads exactly: "Harrowgate Planning Office, clearance file C-118. Bellwether Lane block, surveyed June 1992. No. 12–18 vacant; no commercial use recorded at No. 14; site listed as storage.". Text on inked paper tape laid along the model edge reads exactly: "Grandmother at No. 16 Bellwether sent me to the bakery before dusk. I counted seven paces to the green door at No. 14, crossed to avoid the crack at No. 15, rang the bell at No. 18, and carried a warm heel of rye home. I wrote this in 2019 for the Bellwether Remembered box.". Text on toothpick label flags standing in the model reads exactly: "14 Green Door Bakery · 15 Colm & Sons · 16 Cho House · 18 Night Bell Repair". Text on small cardboard sign taped to the table skirt reads exactly: "Bellwether Remembered workshop — this model is a shared memory, not an official map.". An older resident lifts the miniature bakery from the wrong doorway and sets it at number fourteen, then presses it down so it meets the painted blue route. A younger resident taps the official caption strip, then the index card, and shrugs. Another resident writes a fresh label and pushes it into the base of the corner house. The group moves a tiny fig tree into the back yard, and someone turns the clearance photocopy face down beside the model.

cases.title_en: A Comma Felt Under the Finger
cases.prompt_en:
At a letterpress proofing table, a blind poet reads an embossed sheet with both hands while a printer aligns a translucent print overlay above the same lines. A braille proof slate, loose metal type and tactile line guides make the relationship between spacing, punctuation and breath physically visible. Text on embossed braille proof with a large-print transcription beneath it reads exactly: "NIGHT FERRY — proof 3
The river keeps no doorway,
yet every oar returns a name.
I count the lamps by warmth,
not commas, before the shore answers.
— poem by Lena Marr". Text on tactile line-four proof strip beside the poet's left hand, rendered with visible braille dots and raised texture, reads exactly: "LINE 4 CELLS
I / count / the / lamps / by / warmth / , / not / commas
Query: punctuation cell after WARMTH creates two pauses. Keep or remove?". Text on poet's response card in the correction tray reads exactly: "REMOVE the comma after WARMTH in braille and print. The line should carry one breath into NOT COMMAS. Do not alter the comma after DOORWAY. — Lena". Text on dual-format approval slip attached to the press proof reads exactly: "PROOF 4 APPROVED
Braille cells checked by LM
Print punctuation checked by AR
Line breaks synchronized: YES
Edition credit: poem and final punctuation by Lena Marr". The poet pauses at the fourth line, locates an extra punctuation cell by touch, and asks the printer to remove the matching comma from the metal type. They align both versions again and stamp the approval slip only after the tactile and printed pauses agree.

cases.scene_type: stage magician's notebook reveals collaborative authorship
cases.title_en: The Catch That Took the Bow
cases.prompt_en: A single continuous rehearsal room holds a worn illusion cabinet with its door swung open and a wooden worktable beside it. Stage magician Calder Vale stands at the open cabinet door; prop maker Mara Osei stands at the same worktable. A brass-framed card is fixed to the outside of the cabinet door, an open working notebook lies on the table, a penciled inscription runs along an inner wooden slat of the cabinet, and a small printed attribution card is at the pocket on the cabinet's inner frame. Text on brass-framed patter card fixed to the outside of the cabinet door reads exactly: "Tonight, my own invention — The Vanishing Wardrobe — a mystery I built with my own hands.". Text on open working notebook on the wooden worktable reads exactly: "Cabinet constructed by Mara Osei, mechanic, 1948. Calder wrote the script, chose the silk, and took the bows. The hinge pivot and catch that make the vanish possible were Osei's. Public credit never matched the work.". Text on inner wooden slat of the cabinet beside the hinge pivot reads exactly: "OS-WARD-48 / pivot no.3 / oil before cue / silent count of seven.". Text on small printed attribution card slipped into the pocket on the cabinet's inner frame reads exactly: "The Vanishing Wardrobe. Devised by Calder Vale and Mara Osei. Illusion mechanism designed and built by Mara Osei, 1948.". The prop maker turns a page of the working notebook on the table, taps a penciled correction in the margin, then slides a small printed attribution card into the pocket on the cabinet's inner frame. cases.scene_type: tabletop role-playing campaign archive becomes collective literature
cases.prompt_en: In a small bindery at night, a single long archive table stands under one work lamp, its surface unbroken from one end to the other. Four distinguishable players sit around that same table: a grey-haired woman at the left, a bearded man across from her, a bespectacled younger woman at the right, and a man with rolled sleeves at the far end. The shared tabletop holds, together in one plane, a large hand-drawn fantasy map weighted by a brass handbell and a flat stone; an open campaign chronicle with a mounted old paper letter on its left page and a ruled session record on its right page; a few loose journal pages beside the book; and a hand-sewn chapbook lying open next to the chronicle with its title page facing up. Nothing on the table is separated into frames, stands, or separate display cells. Text on aged paper letter mounted inside the left page of the open campaign chronicle reads exactly: "Mireva of the Ash-Road, to the cartographers who crossed after the flood. The bell proved you were there, and the old ledger was wrong, not the river.". Text on ruled session entry on the right page of the same open campaign chronicle reads exactly: "Session 14 / Graywater Bridge / Watch 11 / Bell rang once / Ferry carried four / No roll defeated the river.". Text on margin of the same right page, written in two ink colors reads exactly: "Ari wrote: “the bridge fell at dawn.” I wrote back: “No, the ledger failed.”". Text on title page of a hand-sewn chapbook lying open beside the campaign chronicle reads exactly: "The Thornfoot Epilogue — Four hands, one river.". The grey-haired woman flips the campaign chronicle to the page with the mounted letter and sets the flat stone on the letter. The bearded man writes a short correction with a second ink color in the margin beside the ruled session entry. The bespectacled younger woman touches that margin correction with a fingertip, then points to the closing line of the mounted letter. The man with rolled sleeves lifts the hand-sewn chapbook, turns its title page toward the lamp, reads it, and puts it back beside the open chronicle on the same tabletop.

cases.prompt_en:
In a quiet study room with paper scrolls hanging on the walls, a young student stands beside a low wooden table. On the table lies a large sheet of xuan paper with rows of Chinese characters written by the student. An older teacher, holding a brush dipped in red ink, leans over the sheet, about to make annotations. The room is lit by warm light from a paper lantern, and other practice sheets are stacked to the side. Text on Student practice sheet reads exactly: "永和九年，岁在癸丑，暮春之初，会于会稽山阴之兰亭，修禊事也。
暮春者，春服既成，冠者五六人，童子六七人，浴乎沂，风乎舞雩，咏而归。
右军此帖，气韵生动，笔势遒媚。余今晨临摹三遍，觉其转折处尚欠圆融。夫子尝言，学书先贵立品，品高则笔自雅。吾当勤习永字八法，以求笔笔中锋。
余细观此帖，羲之运笔如行云流水。今所临“永”字，点画尚欠精到。录其要旨：永字八法者，点为侧，横为勒，竖为努，钩为趯，提为策，撇为掠，短撇为啄，捺为磔。书时须心正笔正，落纸云烟，勿使笔毫散乱。
今临至“惠风和畅”，觉其行气贯通，然“畅”字之撇捺尚觉滞涩。取张怀瓘《书断》所言“笔断意连”之旨，当以虚引实，方得右军之韵。". Text on Teacher's red annotation on margin reads exactly: "此字中锋圆劲，然提按不足，王体精髓在腕活。
用笔之法，贵在藏锋。此字起笔宜逆入平出，收笔回锋。
另：此字戈法稍弱，出钩宜蓄势上挑，如长空新月。
此数字中锋尚可，然牵丝处欠虚灵。王字贵在映带左右，行气一贯。尔临兰亭，当先求形似，后追神韵。留意其藏锋、逆势、回锋诸法，日课不辍，方有所成。". Text on Model inscription hanging on wall reads exactly: "兰亭序·神龙本
临此本需参以冯承素摹本，细察牵丝映带。
神龙本为唐摹，钩摹精细，锋芒毕现。临写时须观其起收笔势，仿其牵丝映带，不可失其风神。
冯摹本中锋转折处最见功力，临写时须留意提按缓急。". The teacher points to a specific character on the student's sheet, then writes a small annotation in red ink beside it. He then gestures to a model inscription hanging on the wall, explaining a historical stroke pattern. The student nods while holding a brush.

In a backstage dressing room of a traditional theater, a performer sits in front of a mirror with makeup brushes and paint pots. cases.prompt_en:
An alley is decorated with colorful handmade lanterns hanging on strings overhead. Families walk and pause beneath them. A wooden table near an entrance holds an answer ledger and a brush. A welcome board stands at the alley entrance. The lanterns sway slightly in the breeze. Text on Lantern riddles reads exactly: "一川橫贯，两岸孤直，无翼而飞，见者皆谜。(打一字)
一船载米，一船载盐，两头尖尖。
一轮明月挂中天，三五良宵共团圆。
四四方方一座城，里面住着百万兵，只见兵打仗，不见兵出城。
红纸灯笼下系谜笺，字迹娟秀。另有灯谜数则，或咏物，或拆字，皆寓吉祥之意。猜者须细心揣摩，不可妄猜。
另有谜云：“此物生来圆又亮，夜晚行路最帮忙，家家户户都需它，一到天明就下岗。”". Text on Answer ledger reads exactly: "谜底：川——三笔相映，象形若流
谜底：菱。
谜底：明月之情，团圆之意。
谜底：蜂巢。
今夜猜谜者众，已录得以下谜底：灯谜一谜底为“川”，因其三笔横竖相映，似水流之形；灯谜二谜底为“菱”，取其两头尖尖之貌；灯谜三乃咏“明月”，寓团圆之意；灯谜四为“蜂巢”，因其内藏万兵，进出忙碌，恰似兵士守城。
谜底为灯笼，取其光照黑夜、夜行引路之用，诚与灯节相契。
灯谜五谜底：“竹”，因其中空有节，似君子谦逊；灯谜六谜底：“墨斗”，木匠用以取直，暗喻规矩。
灯谜七谜底：“秤”，权衡轻重，持家以平；灯谜八谜底：“伞”，能屈能伸，遮风挡雨。
灯谜九谜底：“钟”，晨昏报时，警醒世人；灯谜十谜底：“镜”，正衣冠，明得失。
另有灯谜数十则，谜底或为日常器物，或为自然风物，皆含劝勉之意，望猜者細味。". Text on Welcome board at alley entrance reads exactly: "元宵灯谜会·欢迎猜射
今晚共悬百谜，猜中三谜可领花灯一盏。
孩童需大人陪同，灯下勿近火烛。
灯谜会设于坊巷，以彰文雅。凡猜中者，持谜笺至账房对奖。孩童须由大人带领，共赏花灯。
灯谜会规则：每户限猜五谜，多猜不计；谜底须当面揭晓，中者当场记录。". A parent reads a riddle on a lantern aloud to a child, while another person writes the answer in the answer ledger. An elderly visitor points at a lantern and smiles, and a girl runs from one lantern to another. The welcome board is visible in the background.

cases.title_en: Classical Raga Lesson with Notation and Annotation
cases.prompt_en:
A rehearsal room in a music school. A singing teacher stands beside a wooden notation board, holding a chalk. On the board, five ascending phrases are written in staff notation with Arabic numerals below, and red chalk marks outline the grace-note pattern. A student sits cross-legged with a paper lyric sheet in Hindi, and the tabla player has a small card with the tala cycle. Text on wooden notation board reads exactly: "Raga Yaman – Arohana: N R G M P D N S' | Ornament: Mind (grace)
Avaroha: S' N D P M G R S | Vadi: G, Samvadi: N | Jati: Sampurna-Sampurna
Second phrase: M G R S. In Yaman, R is komal (flat), giving the raga its signature. The mind (grace) typically touches the vadi G with oscillation.". Text on lyric sheet reads exactly: "जो तुम तन मन ध्यावो | श्री राम सदा सहायो
तान: सा रे ग म प ध नि सां | आलाप: सा रे सा
ध्यान से गाओ, स्वर साफ रखो।". Text on tala card reads exactly: "Teental: 4+4+4+4 | Sam on 1
Vibhag: dha | kha | ga | dha | Bols: dha dhin dhin dha | dha dhin dhin dha | dha tin tin ta | ta dhin dhin dha". The teacher taps the board at the second phrase and sings a short ascending figure, then circles the grace-note mark. The student sings the phrase back, slightly flat, and the teacher nods and underlines a numeral while explaining. The tabla player counts a 16-beat cycle and the student joins again with more accurate ornamentation.

Second phrase: M G R S. In Yaman, R is komal (flat), giving the raga its signature. The mind (grace) typically touches the vadi G with oscillation.

A woodblock printing workshop in an old town. The master printer inks a carved block on a workbench while an apprentice, holding a printed almanac sheet, points to the seasonal sayings section. 曲目：铁桥公传奇 第七、八折

本折乃高潮所在，水怪现身，英雄救民，听者动容。". The bard shuffles through the cue cards, mentally rehearsing the sequence of episodes. He points to one card and asks the musician to remember the refrain for that emotional turning point. The musician nods and hands him the refrain sheet to recheck the exact wording.

A wooden fishing boat rests on timber props in a harbor-side yard. The hull bears a fresh carved inscription. An elder in a deep blue ceremonial coat holds a long red blessing scroll. Family members knot colored ribbons onto the bow rail. Nearby, a wooden registry lies open beneath a lantern. Text on hull inscription reads exactly: "顺风顺水·满载而归

潮起潮落，佑我舟航。
今有信士余家，敬造新舟，名曰海安。船身坚固，桅帆高张。伏望妈祖垂怜，四海波平。开船之际，牲醴齐备。舵公虔诚，水手齐心。撒網得利，归来有期。更祈船員平安，合家歡聚。神恩浩荡，永世不忘。

船員齊聲三呼，鑼鼓齊鳴，彩帶紛飛，船身徐徐入水。眾皆歡呼，祈禱海晏波平。

協力同心，滿載而還。
仪式：主祭燃香三炷，献酒三巡，撒米祈福。". The elder unrolls the blessing scroll and reads the invocation aloud. As he reads, a young woman ties a yellow ribbon onto the bow rail. A boy points at the hull inscription as the elder's voice rises and falls with the chant.

Inside a sunlit tile workshop, an artisan stands beside a large wooden worktable. On the table lies a detailed geometric construction diagram drawn on parchment, showing a 12-pointed star formed by intersecting circles and lines, with labeled points and proportions. Behind the artisan, a corkboard displays a pattern glossary with sketches of motifs like 'Baku Star', 'Carpet Medallion', and 'Rose of the Desert', each with a short description. A placard on the wall reads:. The apprentices, holding pencils and compasses, gather around the table. Text on parchment construction diagram reads exactly: "12-POINT STAR | method: divide circle into 12 | key: A-B-C-D-E-F
Step 1: Draw a circle and divide into 12 equal parts using 30-degree angles. Step 2: Label points A through F at alternating vertices. Step 3: Connect every fourth point to form the star's inner and outer rings. The proportion of outer radius to inner radius is 2 to 1.". Text on corkboard pattern glossary reads exactly: "Baku Star (Caucasus) – protection; Carpet Medallion – lotus & renewal; Rose of the Desert – five-fold symmetry, wedding chests.". Text on wall placard reads exactly: "School of Geometric Arts — Est. 1892
Principles: Precision, Harmony, Heritage. Founded by Ustad Karim al-Baku, master of the Caucasus school.". The artisan points with a wooden pointer at the construction diagram and traces the star's outer circle. One apprentice leans forward to examine the glossary, while another checks her own drawing against the diagram. The artisan then draws a new line between two labeled points and explains how the pattern connects to regional design vocabulary.

In a quiet sunlit room, a row of low wooden tables. On the nearest table lies a broken ceramic bowl colored dark blue, its fragments already joined with gleaming gold lacquer lines. Next to the bowl rests an open paper ledger, its pages filled with handwriting and small sketches. On the wall above the table hangs a cork board with a handwritten process guide and polaroid photos of repaired vessels. Small jars of gold powder and brushes line the tabletop. Text on repair ledger reads exactly: "欠けた記憶を金で繋ぐ: The bowl we repair still holds the story.

Dipping a fine brush into gold-tinged lacquer, she traces a hairline crack to perfect the seam, then sets down the brush. cases.prompt_en:
A sunlit room in a rural home. An elderly grandmother and her adult granddaughter sit at a wooden table with an old embroidered cloth spread out. The cloth displays rows of traditional motifs: a pine tree, a crane, a lotus, and a pair of fish, each with tiny Chinese characters stitched beneath. A small handwritten note card lies beside the cloth, describing a new motif to add. The grandmother points to a symbol, while the granddaughter holds a needle and thread. Text on embroidered cloth reads exactly: "松鹤延年
莲年有鱼
松: 常青、長寿、不変。鶴: 千年を生き、天と地を結ぶ。蓮: 清らかさ、泥より出でて染まらず。魚: 豊穣、調和、余裕。
松鶴同春，寓意長壽與吉祥；蓮年有魚，諧音「連年有餘」，祈求年年富足。
鶴壽千年，松柏長青，蓮出淨水，魚躍有餘。
松针四季常青，象征长寿；鹤飞九天，寓意高洁；莲花出淤泥而不染，表清白家声；双鱼戏水，愿子孙绵延，年年有余。
松樹象徵長壽，鶴鳥代表高潔，蓮花喻清白，雙魚兆豐年，四紋合為“壽、潔、清、裕”。
祖母指紋樣，歷數家史：松為祖輩手植，鶴為遷居祥兆，蓮出於祖宅池塘，魚盼年年有餘。
繡法以平針、套針、打籽繡為主，線色深淺過渡，恰如水墨暈染。
邊框處預留空位，將補繡梅瓣五朵，每瓣藏一“福”字，合“五福臨門”之吉。
祖母囑咐：紋樣不僅求美，更承家訓——守正、篤學、勤儉、和睦、知恩。". Text on handwritten note card reads exactly: "梅开五福
梅開五福: 梅花五瓣、それぞれ福禄寿喜財を表す。冬に咲き、希望と再生の象徴。この縁取りに加える。
今日補繡梅瓣，願家人平安、事業順遂，福氣隨春而至。
五福臨門，春滿庭院。
今補梅花，表吾家願。
梅花寒冬綻放，寓堅韌不拔；五瓣象徵五福，繡入布緣，願家族綿延，福澤長久。
紙箋角落畫有小梅枝，旁註：取東坡“梅破春近”之意，繡時須留意花瓣向背。". The grandmother explains the meaning of each motif as she points with her finger, tracing the pine tree, crane, lotus, and fish symbols. The granddaughter listens and then looks at the note card, which shows a sketch of a plum blossom and the words (plum blooms with five blessings). She picks up the needle and begins to stitch a new plum blossom motif onto the cloth's border, while the grandmother watches approvingly.

cases.title_en: The Family Stamp: A Ceremonial Bread Gathering
cases.prompt_en:
In a rustic bakery's stone-walled workshop, three generations of bakers gather around a long oak table. A wooden stamp index rack displays carved stamps with handles shaped like wheat sheaves. On the table, a linen-covered board holds rows of unbaked dough rounds, each brushed with egg wash. A chalkboard menu on the wall lists the day's specials. The morning light filters through a dusty window. Text on wooden stamp index rack reads exactly: "Harvest Blessing · Midsummer Swirl · Ancestor Knot · New Dawn Braid
Harvest Blessing: wheat sheaf design for the autumn gathering; Midsummer Swirl: spiral honoring the sun's peak; Ancestor Knot: interwoven lines remembering family roots; New Dawn Braid: three-strand plait for the spring renewal.". Every stamp carries its story: the Harvest Blessing feeds the hungry, the Midsummer Swirl marks the longest day, the Ancestor Knot binds generations, and the New Dawn Braid welcomes the new season. Families bring their own stamps to imprint their prayers.". Text on dough board (linen cover) reads exactly: "Pressed with love, risen with faith
Each loaf carries a family's blessing for the table.". The eldest baker lifts a carved stamp from the rack, presses it into a dough round, then hands it to a young woman who sprinkles coarse salt over the imprinted loaf. A middle-aged man consults a handwritten gathering notice and reads aloud the occasion each stamp represents. They discuss the sayings carved on the handles.

cases.title_en: Gilding the Name: An Apprentice's Lesson
cases.prompt_en:
A sunlit workshop with high ceilings is filled with the scent of varnish and linseed oil. The master sign painter stands before a large wooden storefront sign propped on easels, its surface coated with red sizing. The apprentice, wearing a smock, watches closely. Nearby, a workbench holds numbered jars of gold leaf and a handwritten technique card. A sketch sheet with the storefront lettering and flourishes lies beside the sign. Text on storefront sign reads exactly: "VELVET & VINE — Established 1923 — Purveyors of Fine Hats
Velvet & Vine: Since 1923, we have outfitted the city's finest gentlemen and ladies with hats crafted from the softest velour and the most resilient straw, each blocked by hand and finished with silk ribbons.". Text on technique card (handwritten card) reads exactly: "Sizing: 4 hours tack · Leaf: sealer first · Shadow: dry brush
Sizing must reach a tack of four hours before leaf will adhere; always apply a sealer to the sized surface, then lay each leaf with a gentle touch, and finish the letter with a dry-brush shadow to give depth.". Text on sketch sheet reads exactly: "Keep the 'V' strong, let the vine twine
Let the V rise with bold diagonal force while the vine curls softly around it, in the spirit of our house style.". The master uses a gilder's tip to lift a delicate square of gold leaf, presses it onto the sized letter, and burnishes it with a soft brush. He points to the technique card, explaining the sequence of sizing, leafing, and shadowing. The apprentice traces the letterforms on the sketch sheet with a graphite stick.

Text on 3x5 index card taped to the wall below the thermostat reads exactly: "Noah — Leak found Sat 6:15 above blue tape. I closed both shutoffs under Mara's sink. Stain passed pencil line by Monday. Keep towels on floor line; do not use upstairs tub until Dave fixes drain. Call if drip returns before you open valve. —Yuki". Noah crouches below the sink, reads the tag on the left valve, and turns its handle clockwise. He then picks up the folded towels and places them along the drawn boundary on the floor, following the graph-paper sketch on the bookshelf.

A handwritten note card is pinned above the machines, a sewn care label is visible inside the blouse collar, a paper sign-up card is clipped to the washer, and a fabric tag hangs from a white basket nearby. A neighbor stands by the open washer, looking at the blouse inside. Text on handwritten note card pinned above the washers reads exactly: "For whoever sees this. I left my dusty-rose silk blouse in a white basket by Machine 2 after treating a coffee stain on the collar. It is delicate. Do NOT run hot or spin. Please set Machine 3 to Cold + Delicates + No Spin, add gentle soap from the shelf, and write below. — Mara, Apt 4C". Text on sewn care label inside the blouse collar reads exactly: "100% silk. Dry clean only. Cool iron. No bleach. Do not tumble.". Text on paper sign-up card clipped to the washer reads exactly: "Laundry sign-up. Monday 7:30 M. 4A; 8:15 L. 2B; 9:00 P. 5C. Start only your slot.". Text on fabric tag tied to a white basket reads exactly: "Mara 4C — silk blouse — coffee stain — vinegar + cold water — no dryer". The neighbor reaches into the washer to lift the blouse, checks the sewn care label and the handwritten note, reads the sign-up card to confirm whose load was spinning, then resets the dial on the other washer to a cold, gentle, no-spin program, places the blouse in the white basket, and writes a reply line on the note card.

cases.prompt_en: Inside a living room, a family of four is gathered around a large freshwater aquarium on a wooden stand. The water is slightly cloudy and a faint green algae film covers parts of the glass. A small dry-erase board sits on the stand, and a laminated care sheet is taped to the hood. An open spiral logbook rests on the edge of the stand beside a siphon hose and a water-conditioner bottle. A sticky note is attached to the lid above the waterline. Text on Dry-erase board on the aquarium stand reads exactly: "FEED EVERY OTHER DAY — SKIP FRIDAY". Text on Laminated care sheet taped to the hood reads exactly: "TWENTY PERCENT WATER CHANGE EVERY SUNDAY. VACUUM GRAVEL. WIPE INSIDE GLASS. RINSE FILTER SPONGE IN REMOVED TANK WATER. NEVER WASH FILTER SPONGE UNDER TAP WATER.". Text on Handwritten logbook open on the stand reads exactly: "Tue Oct 8 — Pearl hovered near surface. Did early 25% water change. Removed 20 L. Added 10 mL conditioner. Rinsed siphon. Next change: Sun Oct 13.". Text on Water-conditioner bottle label reads exactly: "WATER CONDITIONER — Removes chlorine and chloramine. Dose: 5 mL per 10 gallons. Add to fresh water before refilling.". Text on Sticky note on the tank lid reads exactly: "RINSE SIPHON BEFORE REUSE — NO SOAP". Noticing the cloudy water and the algae on the glass, the teenager calls the rest of the family over. One parent inspects the laminated care sheet while another reads the most recent logbook entry, which records an early water change from Tuesday after a fish appeared stressed. The family compares those dates with the feeding rules on the dry-erase board and with the dose printed on the water-conditioner bottle. They then mix the conditioner into a bucket of fresh water, use the siphon to remove part of the tank water, and refill the aquarium. When the new logbook entry is written in, the teen erases the old feeding schedule on the board and writes a corrected schedule that all four agree on.

Text on Printed airline restriction card on the rug reads exactly: "CARRY-ON LIMIT: 7 KG MAX. MEDICATION MUST BE ACCESSIBLE IN CABIN BAG. FRAGILE ITEMS PACKED IN CENTER. CHECK-IN BAG ALLOWED 23 KG. EXCESS WEIGHT INCURS FEES.". Text on Handwritten note on the digital scale display reads exactly: "LARGE CASE: 24.5 KG (OVER). SMALL CASE: 4.2 KG (OK). NEED TO MOVE 1.5 KG FROM LARGE TO SMALL. They remove a stack of hardcover books and a pair of hiking boots from the large case and place them into the smaller carry-on. cases.scene_type: friends agree on a hiking turnaround point
cases.prompt_en: Three hikers stand by a wooden shelter on a forested ridge. A paper topographic map lies open on a picnic table, marked with handwritten arrows and circled place names. A weather note in a clear plastic sleeve hangs from a backpack strap, and a trail-register box with a pinned ranger note is fixed to the shelter post. Backpacks rest against the bench, and a whistle hangs from the post. Text on notebook page pinned under a stone on the shelter shelf reads exactly: "Copper Ridge turnaround: if we reach Farnham Meadow after 13:40, no Black Peak. Descend the old logging road and catch Marta's 16:10 shuttle. First one back writes the time.". Text on plastic-sleeved weather card clipped to a backpack strap reads exactly: "Afternoon rain at 15:30. Temp drops to 9°C on the ridge. Winds 40 km/h above tree line.". Text on pinned ranger note inside the trail-register box reads exactly: "Black Peak trail washed out 1.4 km past Farnham Meadow. Ranger Dan, June 4.". Text on paper topographic map on the picnic table reads exactly: "Marta's shuttle — 16:10 / Copper Gate / Farnham Meadow — actual 13:42". One hiker checks a wristwatch, then scribbles the current time beside the meadow label on the map. A companion reads the agreed rule aloud from the notebook page, taps the pinned ranger note, and gestures downhill along the old road. The group shoulders their packs and turns away from the upper peak, following their prearranged turnaround condition.

cases.prompt_en: A sunlit backyard patio where two adults and two children are repairing a deflated blue inflatable paddling pool. The pool lies flat on the concrete. A small cardboard patch kit box sits open. A white card with handwritten instructions is propped against the pool wall. A piece of cardboard with a soap-water mixture and a brush lies nearby. A yellow sticky note is taped to the pool's side. Chalk circles mark specific spots on the pool surface. One spot has a small patch applied, but the edge is lifting. Another spot has a larger, fresh patch being smoothed down by an adult's hand. Text on White instruction card propped against pool wall reads exactly: "PATCH PROTOCOL: 1. Dry surface completely. 2. Apply glue, wait 2 mins. 3. Place patch, press 30 secs. 4. Soap test: bubbles = leak. No bubbles = sealed. Wait 4 hours before filling.". Text on Chalk circle on pool surface near lifting patch reads exactly: "LEAK A: Small puncture. Patch lifted. Re-dry and re-test.". Text on Chalk circle on pool surface near fresh patch reads exactly: "LEAK B: Larger tear. New patch applied. Soap test: NO BUBBLES. Sealed.". Text on Yellow sticky note on pool side reads exactly: "WAIT: Do not fill until 4 PM. Both leaks sealed. Sun helps cure glue. Kids: stay off pool until then!". Text on Cardboard patch kit box reads exactly: "AQUA-FIX: Vinyl Repair Kit. 5 Patches. Glue. Sandpaper.". The adult applies soap water to the first patch, watching for bubbles. Seeing none, they move to the second, larger patch, smoothing it firmly. They check the yellow note, then write a new time on it. The children watch intently, waiting for the pool to be ready for the afternoon swim.

cases.scene_type: birthday scavenger hunt repaired after a clue goes missing
